interest: This file provides valuable insight into the early post-World War II economic rehabilitation of occupied Japan under SCAP, specifically the reactivation of the cultured pearl industry as an export commodity to generate foreign exchange. It illustrates the lobbying efforts of private American luxury firms, such as the Imperial Pearl Syndicate, seeking to embed industry experts within government procurement bodies like the United States Commercial Company to influence valuation and supply chains. Furthermore, the correspondence documents the State Department's resistance to commercial conflicts of interest and outlines the quantitative transition of pearl sales from Allied military Post Exchanges (PX) in 1946 to regular international commercial export channels in 1947.
overview: This file comprises correspondence from January and February 1947 between Jos Goldstone, President of the Imperial Pearl Syndicate, and Major General J. H. Hilldring, Assistant Secretary of State, regarding the assignment of an industry technical expert to the United States Commercial Company in occupied Japan. Goldstone offered the services of Miss Theresa Jakobson, a cultured pearl specialist with ten years of experience, on a four-month leave of absence to assist with grading, valuing, and classification in the Japanese cultured pearl trade. Assistant Secretary Hilldring declined the proposal to prevent setting a precedent for private commercial favoritism, while assuring Goldstone that SCAP and the War Department had the reactivation of Japan's cultured pearl industry well in hand, projecting 500,000 grams of pearls for regular commercial export in 1947 following wartime disruptions and initial sales through military Post Exchanges.

subfiles.about: The Imperial Pearl Syndicate offers the services of cultured pearl expert Theresa Jakobson to assist the United States Commercial Company in Japan.
subfiles.from: Jos Goldstone (President, Imperial Pearl Syndicate, Inc.)
subfiles.summary: Jos Goldstone, President of the Imperial Pearl Syndicate, writes to Assistant Secretary of State J. H. Hilldring following up on a recent conversation regarding American commercial involvement in the Oriental cultured pearl sector. Goldstone recommends Miss Theresa Jakobson, a cultured pearl expert with ten years of experience in grading, valuing, classifying, and culturing pearl-oysters who had represented the firm at the New York and San Francisco World's Fairs. He offers to grant Jakobson a leave of absence of up to four months so that she may assist the United States Commercial Company and American cultured pearl importers.

subfiles.about: Assistant Secretary Hilldring declines the Imperial Pearl Syndicate's offer of an adviser and provides an update on the revival of Japan's pearl exports under SCAP.
subfiles.from: J. H. Hilldring (Assistant Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Assistant Secretary of State J. H. Hilldring responds to J. Goldstone, declining the Imperial Pearl Syndicate's offer to loan Miss Jakobson to the United States Commercial Company because doing so would establish a problematic precedent for other commercial firms. Hilldring explains that after discussions with the War Department and a Washington representative of the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP), the revival of Japan's cultured pearl industry is already progressing favorably. He notes that 500,000 grams of pearls are programmed for regular commercial export in 1947, marking a major transition from 1946 when the bulk of pearl stock was sold locally through military Post Exchange (PX) facilities.
